Skill Definition: Read code you did not write, build a model of its intent from its names and structure, and predict its output or final state for a given input.
Explain a programming concept accurately in plain language, using its correct terminology and an example or analogy.
Explain, in writing or aloud, why one piece of code or one sub-problem was solved one way rather than another, naming what the choice buys and what it costs, using concepts from the curriculum.
Reason about how an approach's runtime or memory grows with input size, including the cost of each operation on a data structure, and choose between approaches on that basis.
Write Python that represents data with the built-in types, expresses logic with functions, conditionals and iteration, handles input and errors, and is organized into modules.
Model data and behavior with classes, using encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism where they fit.
Implement a solution to an algorithmic problem using the right data structure and a known pattern, within a stated complexity.
Build an accessible, responsive page with HTML, CSS and a templating language.
Build a server that handles requests, renders responses, consumes external APIs, and organizes its routes, models and views.
Create tables, write queries with joins and aggregates, and connect an application to its database.
Ask a stakeholder the questions that reveal the real constraints behind a request, and record the requirements that result.
State what the first version must do and what it will not, separate must-have from nice-to-have, and say what "done" means before building.
Order the work by importance, dependency and available time, and explain the order.
Describe who the software is for and what they will actually do with it, and let that description decide the design.
Organize code into modules and layers that each have one responsibility, and keep each function at one level of abstraction.

Represent an application's data with the shape that fits it, from a list of dictionaries in a command-line program to a normalized relational schema with its relationships, and justify the shape against the operations the application performs on it.
Design the routes, request and response shapes and error behavior of a server so that a client can rely on them.
Design so that the next change is cheap, and add a feature to an existing codebase without breaking what it already does.
Choose the tool or approach that fits this problem from the options available, and justify the choice against the alternatives.
Judge a piece of code or a proposed solution for readability, simplicity and fit for its purpose, and justify the judgment with curriculum concepts.
Write an instruction precise enough that a model produces the intended artifact, naming the task, the constraints, the context and the expected output.
Break a piece of work into units a model can execute reliably, and say why that unit size.
Decide what a model receives, what persists across sessions and what is left out, and recognize when a session has degraded and needs a reset.
Detect when generated output exceeds what was asked, and reject the excess rather than accept it.
Steer wrong output toward right output without restarting, and recognize when restarting or typing it yourself is cheaper.
Find the defects in generated code that is well named, well formatted and subtly incorrect, at the obvious, subtle and architectural tiers.
Read a traceback from the bottom up to name the error type, the failing line and the call that supplied the value, and state the cause.
Reproduce a failure in code you did not write, form a hypothesis, isolate the cause with a targeted check, and repair it minimally while preserving the rest.
Judge whether a piece of code satisfies a stated requirement, and name what is missing or extra.
Decide what to test and at what level, write tests that prove it, and say what a passing test does and does not show.
Identify the empty, missing, oversized and malformed inputs a function or a program will receive, and handle each one.
Work from the command line to keep a readable history with small commits and clear messages, work on a branch, open and merge pull requests, and resolve a merge conflict.
Implement authentication and authorization, reject hostile input, and manage secrets so that the application resists the common attacks on its stack.
Run the application somewhere real and configure it correctly across development and production with environment variables.
Identify where a system will break as load, data or users grow, and tell the actual bottleneck from the one that feels likely.
Estimate what a design costs to run, including service and token costs, and reduce it without losing what the feature is for.
Write prose that is clear, organized, free of spelling and grammar errors, and rendered as intended.
Name, structure and comment code so that a reader can follow what it does and why, following the language's style conventions.
Write a README, setup instructions and decision notes that let someone else, or a fresh model session, set up, run and extend the project.
Explain and defend the design of an entire system, in writing or aloud, to a technical audience that has not seen it, including decisions made by a model.
Present what was built, for whom and why to a non-technical audience, and translate technical constraints into their terms.
Answer a technical or behavioral interview question aloud with a clear structure and specific evidence from your own work.
Connect an experience, reading, film or discussion to your own identity, values and growth, with specific evidence from your life.
Apply a named concept from the leadership curriculum, such as social identity, intersectionality or socialization, accurately to a case or an experience.
Support a claim with specific evidence and a line of reasoning the reader can follow.
Reason about equity, power and responsibility in a workplace situation and propose a recommendation someone could act on.
Craft a narrative with a throughline, a structure that guides the reader, and development from one part to the next.
Write with correct grammar, spelling and punctuation in a leadership assignment.
Articulate your strengths, values and professional identity, and connect them to the career you are preparing for.
Produce a resume, cover letter or profile tailored to one specific employer or audience.
